corrected_reading: PoisonedRAG scores every baseline on its own outcome: the fraction of target questions answered with the attacker's chosen answer, on NQ with the Contriever retriever and top-5 context (poisonedRAG2024.txt L680-684). Corpus Poisoning does not target answers. Its own paper defines success as 'the percentage of queries for which at least one adversarial passage is retrieved in the top-k results' (poisoningRetrievalCorpora2023.txt L307-311), and for NQ with the same pre-trained Contriever retriever reports top-20 success of 84.2 with a single adversarial passage, 98.1 with ten and 99.4 with fifty (Figure 2, L343-346). PoisonedRAG itself states the reason for the 0.01: the attack 'cannot achieve the generation condition' (L924-926, L1338-1340). Scoring a retrieval attack on an answer-manipulation metric is legitimate inside PoisonedRAG's own harness -- it is what a baseline comparison is for -- but the 0.01 does not license the reading it invites outside it, namely that corpus poisoning does not work. C4 is unmatched; the retrieved sets also differ (top-5 context against a top-20 retrieval metric) and the budgets are of different kinds (5 per-question malicious texts against a global set of query-agnostic adversarial passages), so no common scope exists in either text.
numeric_consequence: The apparent gap is between an answer-manipulation rate and a baseline evaluated on that same metric, so it is internally valid but does not transport: the same attack on the same dataset and retriever is recorded at 0.01 by PoisonedRAG and at 84.2-99.4 by its own authors, because the outcome unit differs. No coordinate-matched cross-paper number exists.
numeric_consequence_short: C4 differs: 0.01 scores answer manipulation, 84.2 scores top-20 retrieval, so no gap is defined.
